query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing an atomically thin, epitaxially aligned tungsten carbide interlayer on tungsten surfaces before copper consolidation will reduce thermal boundary resistance, thereby increasing the effective thermal conductivity of W–Cu composites while preserving their mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional W–Cu composite in which tungsten and copper are consolidated without any specialized interfacial modification.
generation.intervention: Apply an atomically thin, epitaxially aligned tungsten carbide layer onto the tungsten surfaces prior to the copper consolidation step.
generation.conditions: The composite is used in high-temperature, high heat-flux, and high radiation flux environments typical of fusion reactor joints and heat-dissipation applications.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultra‐thin, crystalline tungsten carbide interlayer at the tungsten–copper interface.
generation.mechanism: The tungsten carbide interlayer minimizes phonon scattering by providing a lattice-matched bridge that reduces thermal boundary resistance, while its atomic-scale thickness avoids the formation of bulky, brittle phases that could compromise mechanical or irradiation performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified composite will exhibit an increase in effective thermal conductivity relative to a conventional W–Cu composite, without significant losses in mechanical durability or irradiation resistance under reactor-relevant conditions.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (thermal conductivity, mechanical strength, and irradiation resistance) of standard W–Cu composites with unmodified, random tungsten–copper interfacial structures.
generation.boundary: This benefit should hold at the high operating temperatures and under the neutron and ion irradiation levels encountered in fusion reactors; however, the precise magnitude of improvement may vary with interlayer thickness and interfacial crystallinity.
generation.uncertainty: The extent of the thermal conductivity enhancement is not precisely quantified and may depend on processing conditions and interlayer uniformity. Further assessment is needed to determine optimal interlayer parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of W–Cu composites: one with the atomically thin, epitaxially aligned tungsten carbide interlayer and one conventional reference sample without the interlayer. Subject both batches to identical high-temperature and irradiation (e.g., neutron or ion) conditions representative of fusion reactor environments. Assess thermal conductivity, mechanical strength (stress–strain tests), and irradiation resistance (microstructural analysis post-irradiation).
measurements: Effective thermal conductivity (e.g., via laser flash analysis)
Irradiation-induced damage (e.g., dislocation density, void formation via TEM/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the interlayer-modified composite does not show a statistically significant increase in thermal conductivity relative to the control while simultaneously maintaining equivalent mechanical strength and irradiation resistance under the test conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor aims to study the feasibility of tokamak-type reactors and test technologies and materials for commercial use. One major challenge is developing materials for the reactor’s divertor, which supports high thermal flux. Tungsten was chosen as the plasma-facing material, while a CuCrZr alloy will be used in the cooling pipes. However, the gradient between the working temperatures of these materials requires the use of a thermal barrier interlayer between them. To this end, refractory high-entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying and sintering, and their thermal and irradiation resistance was evaluated. Both alloys showed phase growth after annealing at 1100 °C for 8 days, being more pronounced for higher temperatures (1300 °C and 1500 °C). The VFeTiTaW alloy presented greater phase growth, suggesting lower microstructural stability, however, no new phases were formed. In this context, one of the biggest challenges is the development of structural and functional materials that can withstand the conditions inside the reactor: high temperature, high heat flux, and intense flux of high energy neutrons []. The diverter, located at the bottom of the plasma chamber, where the thermal power from the plasma is exhausted [], is one of the most challenging areas. Tungsten (W), with a high melting temperature, low sputtering rates, low neutron activation, and low tritium and deuterium retention [,], was chosen as the plasma-facing material. CuCrZr alloy was chosen as the heat sink due to its high thermal conductivity and strength. However, there is a gap between the operating temperatures of these two materials. decision.trend: Early work in advanced alloys and composites—especially in tungsten‐based systems for fusion applications—focused on tuning bulk microstructure (via secondary phase additions or refining grain size) and on modifying interfaces by introducing compound layers. In several studies (e.g., on tungsten high-entropy alloys and composites) researchers attempted to improve one performance metric (such as thermal transport or irradiation resistance), but then encountered trade‐offs with toughness or stability at high temperatures and under irradiation. This has led to efforts that modify interfacial bonding to ease heat flow, yet earlier compound layer additions sometimes introduced brittle phases or weak spots. Thus, the field has progressively moved from bulk modification to interface engineering to address the critical issue of thermal boundary resistance while still preserving mechanical and irradiation behavior.
decision.unsolved: Despite improvements in either conduction (via interface modifications) or microstructural stability (via composition and processing adjustments), a single intervention that effectively lowers the thermal boundary resistance between tungsten and copper yet retains the composite’s mechanical integrity and irradiation tolerance has not been demonstrated.
decision.lever: Introduce an atomically thin, epitaxially-aligned high-thermal-conductivity interlayer (for example, a tailored tungsten carbide) on tungsten surfaces prior to copper consolidation
decision.why: This approach leverages the trend of refining interfacial properties to enhance phonon transmission while avoiding bulky compound layers that compromise toughness. An ultra‐thin interlayer can act as a thermally bridging phase that minimizes phonon scattering at the W–Cu interface, aligning with cues from studies on tungsten-based alloys that emphasize interface stability under high temperature and irradiation. The precise control of interlayer thickness and crystallographic orientation should allow improved thermal conductivity without sacrificing the mechanical durability or irradiation resistance required for heat-dissipation and fusion reactor joint applications.
